title: Why Don't Hippos Get Sunburned? 🦛
description:
Why don't hippos get sunburned? Glands under a hippo's skin ooze a clear fluid that turns red, then orange-brown, within minutes; its red and orange pigments (hipposudoric and norhipposudoric acid) soak up UV light like a natural sunscreen, and the red one also stopped bacteria growing in lab tests.

Sources:
https://www.nature.com/news/2004/040524/full/news040524-7.html
https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/207/19/v/14939/HIPPOS-LEAD-THE-WAY-IN-MULTIPURPOSE-SUN-SCREEN
https://www.nature.com/articles/429363a

Animated in the Kawaii Anime style.
pinned_comment: If you could sweat any color, which one would you pick? 🎨
script: Hippos sweat red goo, and you'll never see one sunburned. But why? A hippo spends hours in the African sun, with almost no hair to protect it. So its skin fights back. Glands under the skin ooze a thick, clear goo. Within a few minutes, it turns bright red, then a rusty orange-brown. That's why people call it blood sweat. But it's not blood, and it's not really sweat. The color comes from two pigments, one red, one orange. Together, they soak up ultraviolet light, like built-in sunscreen. And the red one does even more. In lab tests, it stopped nasty bacteria from growing. Handy, when rivals leave scratches all over you. So a hippo makes its own sunscreen, and its own antibiotic. If you could sweat any color, which one would you pick?
key_facts: Hippos secrete a fluid from glands under the skin that is neither blood nor strictly sweat (Nature News 2004; JEB 2004)
It comes out as a thick clear fluid and turns red-brown within a few minutes (JEB); it keeps its red hue for hours (Nature News)
Two pigments: red hipposudoric acid and orange norhipposudoric acid (Saikawa et al., Nature 429, 2004)
The secretion absorbs UV and visible light (200-600 nm), acting as a sunscreen (JEB; Nature News)
In lab tests the red pigment inhibited Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Klebsiella pneumoniae (Nature News); hippos are often scarred from fights, which can get infected (Nature News)
Hippos have very little hair and spend time in direct sunlight (Nature News)
